verses.text: Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
For if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself.
But let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone, and not in another.
For every man shall bear his own burden.
Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things.
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand.
As many as desire to make a fair shew in the flesh, they constrain you to be circumcised; only lest they should suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.
For neither they themselves who are circumcised keep the law; but desire to have you circumcised, that they may glory in your flesh.
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature.
And as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.
From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.
Brethren, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

chapters.summary: Having set the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit, Paul now tests the doctrine on the hardest case a congregation faces, which is what to do with a member who has failed. The instruction is addressed to the very people most likely to enjoy the moment — "ye which are spiritual" — and the verb chosen is medical and reparative rather than punitive: "if a man be overtaken in a fault... restore such an one in the spirit of meekness." The word "overtaken" grants that the man was caught rather than merely calculating, and the corrective is aimed straight back at the corrector: "considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted." From this comes the summary command, "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" — a striking phrase from a writer who has spent five chapters dismantling law as a way of standing before God, and who now names the whole obligation of the Christian community by that word. What follows deflates the self-importance that makes burden-bearing impossible: "if a man think himself to be something, when he is nothing, he deceiveth himself," the deception being self-inflicted rather than imposed by anyone else. The alternative to comparison is examination — "let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone, and not in another" — and it is grounded in a sentence that sits in apparent contradiction to verse two: "every man shall bear his own burden." A brief practical note follows on supporting teachers, "Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things," and then the chapter's central warning, delivered with agricultural bluntness: "Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap." The two harvests are named without softening — "he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting" — and the pastoral application is directed not at the reckless but at the exhausted: "let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not." The scope is then set as wide as opportunity allows, with a priority rather than a boundary: "let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith." At verse eleven Paul takes the pen from his secretary — "Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand" — and the closing paragraph is his own handwriting pressed hard into the page. He assigns a motive to his opponents that is neither theological nor sincere: "As many as desire to make a fair shew in the flesh, they constrain you to be circumcised; only lest they should suffer persecution for the cross of Christ," and he charges them with inconsistency as well as cowardice, since "neither they themselves who are circumcised keep the law; but desire to have you circumcised, that they may glory in your flesh." Against their boasting in other men's bodies he sets the only boast he will make: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world." The formula of the fifth chapter returns in its final form, with the positive term supplied at last — "in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision, but a new creature" — and a benediction is pronounced on those who measure by it: "as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God." Then the last word on the subject, weary and immovable: "From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus." His opponents wanted a mark cut into Gentile flesh; Paul offers the scars already cut into his own. The letter closes with the only thing it has ever been arguing for, "the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen."
takeaways: The chapter opens where communities usually fail, and it does so by aiming the instruction at the strong rather than the fallen. Paul addresses "ye which are spiritual," and the address is not flattery but exposure, since the moment a man accepts that description of himself he is exactly the man most in danger. The prescribed manner, "in the spirit of meekness," is drawn straight from the fruit of the Spirit in the previous chapter, so the correction of a sinner becomes the test case for whether the Spirit is actually producing anything. And the clause that follows, "considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted," abruptly reverses the direction of scrutiny: the one doing the examining is himself under examination, and the singular pronoun after a string of plurals makes it personal. A church that cannot restore gently is not spiritually advanced; it has simply relocated the works of the flesh into its disciplinary procedures.

The apparent contradiction between bearing one another's burdens in verse two and bearing one's own burden in verse five is deliberate rather than careless, and Paul uses two different words for the load. The first is a crushing weight, the kind that flattens a man and requires other hands; the second is closer to a soldier's pack or a traveller's kit, the assigned portion nobody else can carry for him. So the two verses are not in competition but in sequence: precisely because each person will answer personally for his own work, nobody is entitled to hand off responsibility, and precisely because some weights genuinely crush, nobody is meant to carry them alone. The self-deception of verse three sits between the two for a reason — the man who thinks himself something will neither stoop to carry another's load nor honestly examine his own.

Paul's phrase "the law of Christ" ought to stop any reader of this letter. He has spent five chapters insisting that the law cannot justify, that returning to it is bondage, and that those led by the Spirit are not under it; then he names the obligation of mutual burden-bearing as a law and says it is fulfilled by keeping it. The point is not that he has quietly recanted but that he distinguishes two things a law can be. As a system for establishing standing before God it is finished; as the shape a Spirit-formed life takes toward the neighbour it is not only intact but intensified, since bearing someone else's crushing weight is a good deal more demanding than a rite. This is the same move as the previous chapter's summary of all the law in loving the neighbour, and it is the reason Galatians cannot be read as an argument against Christian obligation.

The sowing and reaping warning is aimed at a specific self-flattery: "Be not deceived; God is not mocked." The verb suggests turning up the nose at someone, and the target is the man who supposes that inward disposition and outward outcome can be kept apart indefinitely, that one may sow in one field and harvest in another. Paul's answer is that the moral world is agricultural rather than arbitrary — what is planted determines what comes up, and the interval between the two changes nothing. What is notable is where he then applies it. The application is not a threat aimed at the profligate but encouragement aimed at the tired: "let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not." The same law that makes the flesh's harvest inevitable makes the Spirit's harvest certain, and the only thing at issue is whether one is still standing at the season.

Paul's account of his opponents' motives is unusually specific and unusually unflattering, and it reframes the whole controversy. They want "to make a fair shew in the flesh"; they act "lest they should suffer persecution for the cross of Christ"; they do not themselves keep the law they are pressing; and what they are after is the ability to "glory in your flesh," counting converts as trophies. This turns the dispute from a theological disagreement into a question about the cross's social cost. Circumcising Gentiles kept the churches legible and safe within a recognized religious framework, and it spared the missionaries the trouble that came with preaching an executed messiah to anyone. The offence of the cross, which the previous chapter named directly, is thus not incidental to the gospel but the very thing the compromise was designed to avoid.

The letter ends by replacing one mark in the flesh with another. Paul's opponents want a cut made in Gentile bodies as proof of belonging; Paul answers, "I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus," pointing to the scars left by beatings, stonings and imprisonments incurred for preaching. Both are bodily, both are visible, and both signify allegiance, but one is a credential displayed for advantage and the other is damage taken for a person. The formula of verse fifteen sets the same contrast at the level of doctrine: neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, and what does count is "a new creature" — something made rather than performed, and made by God rather than negotiated. The whole letter comes to rest on that, which is why the last word before the benediction is a request to be left alone about it.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 18:15 — if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone
crossRefs.why: Jesus gives the procedure that Paul gives the temper for. Matthew's escalating steps assume the same goal Paul names, restoration rather than exposure, since the aim of the private word is that "thou hast gained thy brother," and the surrounding material about the ninety and nine leaving to seek one straying sheep sets the emotional register. Read together they answer different halves of the same question: Matthew tells a church how far to go and in what order, Galatians tells the people carrying it out what state they must be in when they do. Peter's follow-up question about the limits of forgiveness, and the answer he receives, guards both passages against being turned into machinery.

crossRefs.label: Romans 15:1 — we then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves
crossRefs.why: Romans supplies the same obligation with the same vocabulary of bearing and the same warning against self-pleasing, but it adds the christological ground Galatians assumes: Christ pleased not himself, and the reproaches of others fell on him. That grounding explains why Paul can call mutual burden-bearing "the law of Christ" rather than merely good practice — it is the reproduction in the community of what its Lord did. Romans also extends the principle from moral failure to differences of conscience and scruple, which broadens the Galatian instruction beyond cases of obvious fault into the ordinary friction of a mixed congregation.

crossRefs.label: Hosea 10:12-13 — sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity
crossRefs.why: The prophets had long treated the moral order as agricultural, and Hosea states both halves of Paul's proverb in a single oracle: an invitation to sow in righteousness and break up fallow ground, and an indictment for having sown wickedness and eaten the fruit of lies. The context is national rather than individual, which is a useful corrective to reading Galatians 6 purely as private morality, and the accusation that Israel trusted in its own way and its many mighty men parallels Paul's charge that his opponents glory in flesh. Hosea also holds the two together as Paul does, with the harvest of judgment and the possibility of a harvest of mercy set side by side and time still running.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 5:17 — if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away
crossRefs.why: This is the fullest expansion of the phrase Galatians uses as its final formula, and it supplies the mechanism. The new creation follows from a death — one died for all, therefore all died — and issues in no longer knowing anyone after the flesh, which is exactly the criterion Paul is applying when he declares circumcision and uncircumcision alike worthless. Corinthians also names the ministry that flows from it, reconciliation, and states the exchange by which the sinless one was made sin for us. Set against Galatians 6, it shows that "a new creature" is not a vague renewal but the specific result of the cross Paul says is his only boast.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 9:14 — the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel
crossRefs.why: Verse six about the taught sharing good things with the teacher is easy to skim past, and Corinthians shows how seriously Paul took the principle even while refusing to use it himself. He argues it from the ox treading out the corn, from the soldier's wages and the vineyard keeper's fruit, and from the Lord's own ordinance, and then declines his right so that the gospel may be free of charge. The two passages together frame material support for teachers as a genuine obligation on the congregation rather than a claim the minister should press, which fits the surrounding Galatian material about doing good especially to the household of faith.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 3:3-8 — we have no confidence in the flesh; what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ
crossRefs.why: Philippians gives the autobiographical version of Galatians 6's closing argument. Paul lists the credentials he could boast in, circumcision on the eighth day at the head of the list, and writes them all off as loss and refuse for the sake of knowing Christ. The verbal overlap is close — glorying, flesh, confidence — and the passage names the same opponents in the same sharp terms. Reading them together clarifies that Paul is not indifferent to what he rejects but is making a considered exchange, and it supplies the personal history behind the flat statement that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 11:23-27 — in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent, in deaths oft
crossRefs.why: The marks Paul says he bears in his body are itemized here: five times the thirty-nine lashes, three beatings with rods, a stoning, three shipwrecks, and the whole catalogue of hunger, cold and danger. The setting is the same as in Galatians, a defence against rivals whose credentials look better on paper, and Paul's response in both places is to boast in what disqualifies him by ordinary reckoning. Placing the passages together explains the force of "let no man trouble me": the scars are not sentiment but evidence, an accumulated record of what preaching the cross without the compromise had already cost him.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading holds the two burdens of verses two and five together as an account of solidarity within one body. Because the members of the Church are genuinely joined in Christ, spiritual goods can really be shared — prayer, penance and satisfaction offered for another are not merely encouraging gestures but a real bearing of a real weight, which is the communion of saints extended to the living and the dead. At the same time each person will answer for his own work, so the sharing of burdens never dissolves personal responsibility or supplies the repentance another must make for himself. The instruction to restore the fallen is read as the pastoral shape of this same conviction, and stands behind the Church's understanding of fraternal correction and of sacramental confession as the ordinary place where a fault is confronted and a brother restored by someone charged to act in meekness rather than in judgment.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters embrace the practical force of burden-bearing while resisting any notion of transferable merit or satisfaction. On their reading verse five sets the limit that verse two must not overrun: each person stands or falls before God individually, no one can discharge another's account, and the two verses use different words precisely to prevent that confusion. Restoration is understood as the work of the whole congregation rather than of a priestly office, with the mutual confession of faults and the ministry of the word as its instruments. Many also note that Paul addresses "ye which are spiritual" to the church at large and not to a class within it, which they take as evidence that the ministry described here is common to believers. Both traditions read the pair of verses as a deliberate tension rather than a contradiction, requiring genuine mutual aid now and expecting genuine personal accountability at the end.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" and the promise that "in due season we shall reap, if we faint not," Catholic interpretation finds a plain statement that God judges according to works and truly rewards them. Life everlasting is here described as a harvest answering to a sowing, which the tradition takes as compatible with grace precisely because the sowing itself is grace at work in a person made genuinely free by it; God crowns his own gifts, and in doing so crowns the real acts of a real agent. This is the scriptural texture behind the doctrine of merit, which does not mean that heaven is purchased but that grace-enabled good works have a true and God-given value and that perseverance in them matters eternally. The warning half of the verse carries the same weight in reverse, since sowing to the flesh reaps corruption, and the whole is offered as a reason not to grow weary rather than as a calculation of wages.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters read the harvest as gift rather than payment, noting that verse eight sets the reaping "of the Spirit" rather than of the sower's effort, so the produce belongs to the one who supplied the seed. The passage is generally taken as describing the organic connection between a life and its outcome, and as evidence at the judgment rather than as the ground of acceptance, which remains the righteousness of Christ received by faith. Many stress that Paul's immediate purpose is pastoral encouragement to the weary and a warning against self-deception, not a doctrine of reward, and they resist merit language as importing a contractual frame Paul nowhere uses. Both traditions insist that the verse forecloses any version of grace that makes conduct irrelevant, and both hear in "God is not mocked" a refusal to let profession stand in for practice.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads "a new creature" as a real ontological renewal rather than a change of standing or of self-understanding, and connects it directly to baptism, where the letter has already located the putting on of Christ. The contrast with circumcision is instructive: Paul does not reject a bodily sign in favour of a purely interior religion but replaces a sign that marked descent with a new birth that actually confers what it signifies. On this reading the new creation is begun sacramentally, grows through the life of grace described in the previous chapter's fruit, and is completed in glory, so the phrase gathers up the whole letter's argument that what matters is what God has made rather than what a person can display. The benediction that follows, pronounced on those who walk by this rule, is understood as extending the peace of the covenant to the community constituted by that new birth.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters affirm the reality of the new creation while generally locating it in regeneration by the Spirit received through faith, and many are cautious about tying it too tightly to the rite, on the grounds that Paul's whole argument here is that no external ceremony avails anything and that tying the new creation to a ritual risks reproducing the error he is combating. Reformed and evangelical readers commonly stress that regeneration is monergistic and instantaneous, distinguishable from the growth that follows. A significant strand also reads the phrase corporately, as the new creation inaugurated in Christ into which believers are brought, rather than primarily as a change in the individual. Both traditions agree that the phrase names something God does rather than something a person achieves or performs, and both take it as the letter's final answer to the question of what actually counts.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "the Israel of God" in verse sixteen as the Church itself, the covenant people now constituted in Christ and including believing Jew and Gentile alike. The context supports it: Paul has just declared circumcision irrelevant and the new creature decisive, and he pronounces peace and mercy on "as many as walk according to this rule," which suggests that the concluding phrase describes the same people rather than a separate group. This is of a piece with the letter's earlier argument that those who are of faith are the children of Abraham, and it underwrites the traditional conviction that the promises made to Israel are not abolished but fulfilled and extended in the Church, without implying that God has withdrawn his fidelity toward the Jewish people or that the covenant with them was a mistake.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings divide sharply. Reformed and covenantal interpreters agree with the Catholic reading and often press it further, treating the Church straightforwardly as the continuation of Israel. Dispensational interpreters argue that the conjunction before the phrase distinguishes rather than identifies, so that Paul pronounces peace on all who walk by the rule and mercy in particular upon believing Jews, whom they take to be the Israel of God; on this view Israel retains a distinct identity and distinct promises still to be fulfilled, and collapsing the two obscures them. Others read the phrase as a deliberate reclaiming of the title against the agitators, who claimed the name of Israel by descent and circumcision. Both traditions agree that the qualifying clause is the operative one, that walking by the rule of the new creation is what defines the people being blessed, and that the blessing is peace and mercy rather than status.
